idea.body: A logarithm undoes an exponent. When x is stuck in the exponent, like in 3^x = 27, a logarithm pulls it back down where you can solve for it. If both sides can be written with the same base, just match the exponents: 3^x = 27 = 3^3, so x = 3. When the bases will not match, take a logarithm of both sides instead. For 3^x = 20, log base 3 of both sides gives x = log_3(20). That is still exact, even though it is not a whole number. The same idea runs in reverse for log equations. log_2(x) = 5 means x = 2^5 = 32. A logarithm and its base's exponential simply undo each other.

figure.alt: A table with x from 0 to 4 next to 3^x, going 1, 3, 9, 27, 81, each one three times the one before.

workedExample.prompt: A robot's battery charge follows C = 20 times 3^t. After how many hours is the charge 540?

ways.name: Match the bases
ways.when: Use this when both sides of the equation can be written as powers of the same base.
steps: Rewrite both sides as powers of the same base.
The bases match, so the exponents must be equal.
ways.trap: Forgetting to rewrite the right side as a power of the same base and just guessing.

ways.name: Take a logarithm of both sides
ways.when: Use this when the bases do not match, like 3^x = 20.
steps: 3^x = 20 has bases that do not match, so use a logarithm.
Take log base 3 of both sides: log_3(3^x) = log_3(20).
The log base 3 and the power 3 undo each other: x = log_3(20).
The answer stays exact as a logarithm.
ways.trap: Trying to match bases when they do not factor into each other, and getting stuck.

ways.name: Solve logarithmic equations by undoing the log
